curriculum.lesson_evidence: Comparing Australia with a neighbouring country uses criteria such as size, climate zones, population patterns and connections (trade, travel), supported by data tables.
curriculum.scope_limit: Proposed Stage 2 NESA HSIE alignment using catalogue outcome codes (HS2-*); content-point mapping and local First Nations protocols remain pending human review.

lesson.child_mission: Comparing Australia with a neighbouring country uses criteria such as size, climate zones, population patterns and connections (trade, travel), supported by data tables.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Choose two criteria to compare Australia with Indonesia and say what source you need for each.

FEEDBACK
e.g. climate zones / population — atlas or statistics agency pages.

WATCH FOR
Declaring one country “better” is not a geographic comparison.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Complete a compare table for Australia and one neighbour across six criteria with sources. Write two similarity and two difference sentences.

Write a short reflection naming one source or idea you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Comparing Australia with a neighbouring country uses criteria such as size, climate zones, population patterns and connections (trade, travel), supported by data tables.
materials: Optional: local map, photo or interview notes
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Complete a compare table for Australia and one neighbour across six criteria with sources. Write two similarity and two difference sentences. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: original example using compare on new material; names a specific word, source or choice and explains its effect.

Parent: Written model 2: Sample error: Declaring one country “better” is not a geographic comparison.. Correction: e.g. climate zones / population — atlas or statistics agency pages.. Why it helps the audience is stated.

Parent: Likely misconception: Declaring one country “better” is not a geographic comparison. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating compare on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with compare, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept original work about compare with a specific supporting detail. Reject copied model wording with no new material. / Accept a misconception, a correction, and a purpose-linked reason for compare. Reject corrections that do not change the inaccurate idea..

teach_steps.explain:
Comparing Australia with a neighbouring country uses criteria such as size, climate zones, population patterns and connections (trade, travel), supported by data tables.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on sources, places and respectful community knowledge, rather than guessing from a single picture. Keep every claim linked to evidence.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the sources, map features or community examples that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a detail is uncertain, identify what source you would need next. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
